note: Upper Canada, the British occupations of Michigan and eastern Maine, the Red Stick Creek country and each raid are drawn as held areas; the lines are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and the cited accounts.

chapters.title: The fall of Detroit
arrows: Hull crosses the Detroit River to Sandwich (12 July 1812)
Roberts sails from St Joseph Island to Mackinac (16–17 July 1812)
Brock and Tecumseh cross to Detroit (15–16 August 1812)
chapters.text: The United States declared war on Britain on 18 June 1812, and on 12 July General William Hull crossed the Detroit River into Upper Canada. A British, fur-trader and Indigenous force from St Joseph Island took Fort Mackinac without a fight on 17 July, and Hull, his supply line harassed by Tecumseh's warriors, pulled back to Detroit in early August. On 15 August Potawatomi warriors destroyed the garrison of Fort Dearborn (Chicago) as it marched out, and the next day Hull surrendered Detroit to Isaac Brock and Tecumseh, leaving Michigan Territory in British hands.

chapters.title: The Niagara frontier, 1812–1813
arrows: Van Rensselaer's crossing at Queenston (13 October 1812)
American landing at York (27 April 1813)
Assault on Fort George (27 May 1813)
American advance to Stoney Creek (1–5 June 1813)
Harvey's night attack at Stoney Creek (6 June 1813)
British capture of Fort Niagara and raid on Lewiston (19 December 1813)
Riall's raid on Black Rock and Buffalo (30 December 1813)
chapters.text: On 13 October 1812 American troops crossed the Niagara River and seized Queenston Heights, but Brock's counter-attack, in which he was killed, and Roger Sheaffe's reinforcements forced them to surrender the same day. In April 1813 the Americans occupied York, the capital of Upper Canada, for nearly two weeks and burned its parliament buildings; on 27 May they stormed Fort George, but defeats at Stoney Creek on 6 June and Beaver Dams on 24 June penned them in around the fort. In December they abandoned it and burned the village of Newark, and the British replied by taking Fort Niagara on 19 December and burning Lewiston, Black Rock and Buffalo.

chapters.title: Lake Erie and the Thames
arrows: Winchester advances to Frenchtown (17–18 January 1813)
Procter's counter-attack on Frenchtown (22 January 1813)
Harrison lands below Amherstburg (27 September 1813)
Johnson's mounted riflemen ride to Detroit (25–30 September 1813)
Procter's retreat up the Thames (27 September – 4 October 1813)
Harrison's pursuit to Moraviantown (2–5 October 1813)
chapters.text: An American column advancing on Detroit took Frenchtown on the River Raisin on 18 January 1813, but four days later Henry Procter's British and Indigenous force destroyed it, and wounded prisoners left behind were killed the next day. In May Procter and Tecumseh besieged Fort Meigs without success. On 10 September Oliver Hazard Perry captured the whole British squadron on Lake Erie, cutting Procter's supply line; the British abandoned Detroit and Amherstburg, and on 5 October William Henry Harrison's army caught them on the Thames near Moraviantown, where Tecumseh was killed. Harrison burned Moraviantown and went back to Detroit, but the Americans kept Amherstburg and Sandwich for the rest of the war.

chapters.title: The Creek War
arrows: Red Stick attack on Fort Mims (30 August 1813)
Jackson's march to Fort Strother and Tallushatchee (October–November 1813)
Jackson relieves Talladega (9 November 1813)
Jackson's march to Horseshoe Bend (14–27 March 1814)
Jackson marches to the Hickory Ground (April 1814)
chapters.text: A civil war inside the Creek Nation became a war with the United States when militia attacked Red Stick warriors at Burnt Corn on 27 July 1813; on 30 August the Red Sticks, who had been armed through Spanish Florida, stormed Fort Mims and killed hundreds of the people sheltering there. Andrew Jackson's Tennessee army marched south, built Fort Strother on the Coosa and won at Tallushatchee and Talladega in November. On 27 March 1814 Jackson's troops and their Cherokee and Creek allies broke the Red Sticks at Horseshoe Bend, and on 9 August he forced the whole Creek Nation, his allies included, to give up about 23 million acres in the Treaty of Fort Jackson.

chapters.title: Chippawa, Lundy's Lane and Fort Erie
arrows: Brown crosses the Niagara and takes Fort Erie (3 July 1814)
Scott's advance to Chippawa and Queenston (4–10 July 1814)
Drummond advances to Lundy's Lane (25 July 1814)
Drummond's advance on Fort Erie (August 1814)
chapters.text: On 3 July 1814 Jacob Brown's army crossed the Niagara and took Fort Erie, and two days later Winfield Scott's brigade beat the British at Chippawa. After holding Queenston for most of July, Brown fell back, and on 25 July the two armies fought into the night at Lundy's Lane, near Niagara Falls, in the bloodiest battle of the war. The battered Americans withdrew to Fort Erie and held it against a British siege from August to September, but on 5 November they blew up the fort and recrossed the river.

chapters.title: The occupation of eastern Maine
arrows: Hardy's squadron takes Moose Island (11 July 1814)
Sherbrooke's expedition to Castine (1 September 1814)
Barrie's raid up the Penobscot to Hampden and Bangor (2–5 September 1814)
Occupation of Machias (September 1814)
chapters.text: On 11 July 1814 a British squadron took Moose Island, at Eastport, whose garrison surrendered without a shot. In September John Sherbrooke's expedition from Halifax occupied Castine, beat the militia at Hampden on 3 September and entered Bangor, while another force took Machias. The British soon left the towns up the Penobscot but held the coast east of the river, under martial law, until after the war.

chapters.title: Bladensburg and the burning of Washington
arrows: Ross marches from Benedict to Upper Marlboro (20–22 August 1814)
Ross marches on Bladensburg and Washington (24 August 1814)
Gordon's squadron sails up the Potomac to Alexandria (17–29 August 1814)
chapters.text: With Napoleon defeated, Britain sent veteran troops to raid the American coast. Robert Ross's force of about 4,500 landed at Benedict on the Patuxent on 19 August 1814, marched by way of Upper Marlboro and on 24 August routed the American militia at Bladensburg. That evening the British set fire to the Capitol, the President's House and other public buildings in Washington, leaving after about 26 hours, while a naval squadron sailed up the Potomac and forced Alexandria to surrender.

chapters.title: Plattsburgh
arrows: Prevost marches on Plattsburgh (31 August – 6 September 1814)
chapters.text: On 31 August 1814 George Prevost led more than 8,000 troops south from Lower Canada along the west shore of Lake Champlain, and on 6 September he reached Plattsburgh, where Alexander Macomb's outnumbered Americans fell back behind the Saranac River. On 11 September Thomas Macdonough's squadron, anchored in Plattsburgh Bay, defeated and captured the British flotilla. Without control of the lake Prevost called off his attack and retreated to Canada that night.

chapters.title: Baltimore
arrows: Landing at North Point and advance on Baltimore (12–13 September 1814)
chapters.text: Three weeks after burning Washington, the British turned on Baltimore. About 4,700 troops landed at North Point on 12 September 1814 and drove back the Maryland militia, but Robert Ross was killed in the fighting. While the army faced the city's earthworks, the fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for about 25 hours on 13–14 September; the fort held, the troops were ordered back to the ships, and Francis Scott Key, seeing the flag at dawn, wrote the verses of 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.

chapters.title: New Orleans
arrows: British boats cross Lake Borgne to the Villeré plantation (22–23 December 1814)
Pakenham's assault on Line Jackson (8 January 1815)
Lambert lands and besieges Fort Bowyer (8–12 February 1815)
chapters.text: A British expedition captured the American gunboats on Lake Borgne on 14 December 1814 and on 23 December landed troops nine miles below New Orleans, where Andrew Jackson attacked them that night. On 8 January 1815 Edward Pakenham's army of about 8,000 assaulted Jackson's earthworks at Chalmette and was cut down, losing about 2,000 men, Pakenham among them, against 71 Americans. The British withdrew and on 12 February took Fort Bowyer at the mouth of Mobile Bay, but news that the Treaty of Ghent had been signed on 24 December arrived the next day, and the war ended when ratifications were exchanged on 17 February.
